title: Gender equality, disability, and social inclusion in the Philippines: Progress, challenges, and opportunities in SDG 5 and SDG 10
authors: Jose Ramon G. Albert, Connie B. Dacuycuy, Agnes R. Quisumbing, Lovelaine B. Basillote, Deanne Lorraine D. Cabalfin, Anna Rita P. Vargas, Paola Ellaine D. Luzon, and Mohammad A. Mahmoud
tldr: Examines Philippines progress on SDG 5 and SDG 10 using intersectional and Shapley decomposition analysis, finding substantial policy achievements alongside critical implementation gaps that perpetuate compound marginalization for women, persons with disabilities, and indigenous peoples.
problem_and_motivation: Despite progressive legal frameworks (Magna Carta of Women, Magna Carta for Disabled Persons, IPRA), women, persons with disabilities, and indigenous peoples in the Philippines continue to face intersecting forms of marginalization that single-identity policies fail to address. The COVID-19 pandemic further exacerbated inequalities, pushing 2.8 million more Filipinos into poverty and disproportionately affecting already vulnerable groups. Evidence-based policy requires comprehensive intersectional analysis of how gender, disability, ethnicity, and geography interact to shape development outcomes.
approach: Mixed-methods design combining quantitative SDG indicator analysis with qualitative key informant interviews and focus group discussions conducted May–August 2025
Shapley decomposition analysis using merged FIES-LFS data (2018, 2021, 2023) to quantify relative contributions of gender, education, geography, and income factors to overall inequality
Intersectional analytical framework examining how gender, disability status, indigenous identity, and socioeconomic position interact to create unique disadvantage patterns
Descriptive data analytics across multiple national surveys including NDHS, LFS, APIS, FIES, NDPS, and the World Bank IP Household Survey
Longitudinal analysis tracking SDG indicator trends from 2015 baseline through 2025 across SDG5 and SDG10 targets
findings: num: 12% of population aged 15+ have disability (15% female vs 9% male), with severe disability prevalence reaching 39% among those with no formal education (55% women vs 23% men) versus 6% among college graduates
num: Women's labor force participation at ~50% vs men at ~74%, with 42% of employed women in vulnerable employment compared to 36.1% of men; 90% of household employees are female
num: Women spend 10–13 more hours per week on housework and care work than men; unpaid care work contributes an estimated 37% of GDP
num: Child marriage before age 18 declined from 16.5% (2017) to 9.4% (2022); only 34% of women experiencing violence sought help
num: BARMM female LFPR increased dramatically from 26.6% (2019) to 54.2% (2023); wealthiest 10% capture 32% of national income
num: Indigenous Peoples comprise 9.46M (8.7% of population); only 22% of 257 approved CADTs were fully registered as of early 2023
num: Women's cabinet representation fluctuated from 36% (2010) to 10% (2019) to 21.1% (2024); WEF rank dropped from 5th (2013) to 20th (2025)
num: Waray speakers show highest disability prevalence (21% overall, 31% women vs 11% men); IP poverty rate at 32.4% in 2023
GAD budget (5% mandatory allocation) has become compliance-oriented rather than transformational, with widespread fund misuse and weak accountability
Statistical invisibility of IPs constitutes the first layer of social, economic, and political exclusion, undermining evidence-based policy development

definitions.definition: Gender Equality, Disability, and Social Inclusion — the condition where all persons have equal rights, equitable opportunities, and fair treatment to contribute to and benefit from development regardless of sex, gender identity, disability, age, ethnicity, religion, or socioeconomic status

Analytical framework recognizing that discrimination and exclusion operate through multiple interconnected systems rather than single characteristics, creating unique patterns of marginalization that cannot be understood through additive approaches

The systematic exclusion of marginalized groups (particularly IPs) from national statistics, constituting the first layer of social, economic, and political exclusion that undermines evidence-based policy
Methodology quantifying the relative contributions of various factors (gender, education, geography, income) to overall inequality patterns using cooperative game theory principles

The phenomenon where multiple forms of disadvantage (e.g., gender + disability + ethnicity + geography) interact to create experiences of exclusion more severe than the sum of individual disadvantages

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper provides the most comprehensive recent assessment of gender equality, disability, and social inclusion in the Philippines using truly intersectional methodology. It demonstrates that single-identity approaches to inclusion are inadequate and that compound marginalization requires integrated policy responses. For the Odin thesis, it establishes the broader socioeconomic context of inequality, labor market precarity, and social protection gaps that shape Filipino young professionals' financial realities. The detailed analysis of social insurance coverage (GSIS/SSS) directly informs understanding of mandated financial obligations as a distinct expense category. The paper's critique of implementation gaps between policy and practice parallels the gap Odin addresses between financial literacy and actual financial behavior.
directly_justifies: The documented gender gap in labor force participation and vulnerable employment justifies attention to income stability as a key behavioral profiling dimension in Odin
GSIS/SSS coverage analysis directly grounds the treatment of government-mandated contributions as obligatory expenses in the budget recommendation module
limits: Does not specifically examine young professionals (20–40 age range), focusing instead on general working-age population
Does not provide individual-level transaction data or spending patterns required for direct ML training
Poverty data is household-level (per capita income) rather than individual-level, limiting intra-household analysis
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: Systematically scanned the 14 topic codes (1.A–14.C) in the Odin topic outline against the paper's content. The paper's primary focus on gender equality, disability, and social inclusion has no exact topic match within the Odin taxonomy, as the thesis centers on personal finance management rather than social development. However, the paper provides essential contextual evidence for: (1) socioeconomic conditions affecting Filipino workers (Topic 1.A), (2) government-mandated financial obligations through GSIS/SSS analysis (Topic 2.A.IV), (3) income inequality as backdrop for financial vulnerability (Topic 8.A.I), and (4) data privacy and regulatory context (Topic 10.A.III). No other topic codes were applicable.

limitations: Official statistics under-represent marginalized populations due to geographic isolation, documentation barriers, and mistrust of government data collection
Small population subgroups (particularly women with disabilities from IP communities) limit robust statistical analysis for intersectional categories
Rapid policy changes during research period make it challenging to isolate effects of specific interventions from broader contextual factors
Study lacked formal IRB approval, though adhered to ethical research principles including informed consent and cultural sensitivity guidelines
Only 4 of 15 national SDG5 indicators have sufficient data; 10 have insufficient data and 1 has no data
Qualitative saturation may have left some highly marginalized subgroups underrepresented
remember_this: Intersectionality: compound > additive disadvantage for women with disabilities/IPs

Gender paradox: women outnumber men 2:1 in professions but face higher vulnerability
